_comment: Level-ceiling recalibration plan. Applied by tools/apply-ceilings.ts.
Each competency area declares a default ceiling; named elements override it.
Expressed this way so the judgement is reviewable in one place rather than
spread across 2104 line edits in 42 files.
THE RULE:
L1  Novice ceiling. Reserved for FOUNDATIONAL areas. Use only where the
competence genuinely stops at following a supplied rule in a framed
situation. Rare, and it should feel wrong before you use it.
L2  Advanced Beginner ceiling. Also foundational. The person applies the
thing in familiar situations and recognises an unfamiliar one, and
there is no Competent tier above that because there is no
unsupervised novel-case practice to have. Definitions, notation and
reading conventions land here.
L3  Competent. Knowledge, vocabulary, institutional structure, conventions,
straightforward technique. The person applies it correctly.
L4  Proficient. Independent practice, non-routine cases, judging the quality
of someone else's routine work. Most technique elements live here.
L5  Expert. A person could plausibly spend a career here and still be
learning, AND a defensible capstone with cross-organizational review is
actually writable. If you cannot describe that capstone, it is not L5.
Areas whose default is 3 are concept and vocabulary areas. Areas whose default
is 4 are practice areas. Nothing defaults to 5 except CM-03-A10 and CM-05-A09,
which are the two genuinely frontier areas in the corpus.
FOUNDATIONAL AREAS default to 3 and override IN BOTH DIRECTIONS. The floor
used to be L3 for everything, which meant the corpus could not express a
competence that genuinely tops out below Competent — and every foundational
element was therefore either inflated to L3 or, as actually happened, left
out of the corpus altogether. L1 and L2 exist for that case.
This said 'override DOWN ... and for no other' until 2026-08-16, and the one
area a practising metrologist graded by hand contradicted it: DP-08-A07
pushed three elements UP to L4 — operating a reference DMM, operating a
nanovoltmeter, and recognising an implausible reading. Foundational is not
shallow (rule 13), so an area is not only a place where ceilings fall, and
an area that comes back with no L4 has probably not been asked the question.
Nine of the ten graded foundational areas currently have no L4 at all.
GRADING A FOUNDATIONAL AREA — the rule, derived from DP-08-A07's overrides.
It does NOT track `kind`: eleven knowledge elements went to L2 there and
twenty-one others were deliberately left at L3.
L2  Knowing what a thing IS. Naming, defining, distinguishing, or a single
computation with one right answer.
L3  Knowing what a thing DOES TO YOUR READING. These titles carry a
consequence clause — 'and why a reading needs to settle'.
L4  Where genuine expertise exists even in a foundational area.
reviewedBy / reviewedOn record that a person actually judged an area. Without
them {"default": 3, "overrides": {}} is ambiguous between 'judged and
uniform' and 'never looked at' — and 21 of 31 foundational areas are in that
state as an artefact of the generated pass, not as 21 separate decisions.
Run `npm run report:foundational` to see which. An area with overrides but no
reviewer is graded-but-unattributed, which is a weaker claim than reviewed.
